Assume full AC. For complex Banach spaces $X,Y$, a bounded complex-linear map $T:X\to Y$ is Fredholm when its range is closed and both $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{coker}T:=Y/\operatorname{ran}T$ are finite dimensional; its index is $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}T:=\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker T-\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T$. Here $L^2$ uses the bundle metric and Riemannian volume, and $H^1$ is the completion of smooth sections in the norm $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2$, equivalent to the finite-chart Sobolev norm. These are complex Hilbert, hence Banach, spaces. A smooth first-order differential operator on this compact base is bounded from $H^1$ to $L^2$. Fredholm and index below refer to this bounded Sobolev realization; the full selfadjoint Dirac operators are separately regarded as unbounded operators on $L^2$ with domain $H^1$.

For the concrete case, set $M=S^4$ with the unit round metric and spin structure induced from the Euclidean ball, take $E=S^+$ with its positive-spin Levi-Civita connection, and use the Clifford action and chiral Dirac operator specified in the round-sphere spin-twist result. Let $z=-I_2\in SU(2)$ be the central gauge automorphism. Write $S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and $t$ for the coordinate on its universal cover. Call the circle spin structure periodic (nonbounding) when lifted spinors satisfy $\psi(t+1)=+\psi(t)$, and antiperiodic (bounding) when they satisfy $\psi(t+1)=-\psi(t)$. If the gauge bundle is glued at the ends by a scalar $\epsilon_g\in\{+1,-1\}$ on $E$ and the spin bundle has multiplier $\epsilon_s\in\{+1,-1\}$, the total spinor section satisfies $\Psi(t+1)=\epsilon_s\epsilon_g\Psi(t)$. In particular, a trivial gauge gluing with periodic spin structure gives periodic total spinors; gluing gauge fibers by $z$ with an antiperiodic spin clutch also gives periodic total spinors, while the same $z$ clutch with periodic spin clutch gives antiperiodic total spinors.

Let $Y=S^4\times S^1$ have product metric and pulled-back gauge connection. On the pulled-back complex bundle $S\otimes E$, put $c_5=i\Gamma$ and $D_5=D_4+i\Gamma\partial_t$, with domain the periodic Sobolev space $H^1(Y;S\otimes E)$, so total spinors obey $\Psi(t+1)=\Psi(t)$. There is a parallel antiunitary involution $J$ preserving $\ker D_5$, and the real skew-adjoint realization $iD_5$ on its $J$-fixed Hilbert space has

$$
\dim_{\mathbb R}(\ker D_5)^J=\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker D_4=1, \qquad \operatorname{ind}_2(iD_5):=\dim_{\mathbb R}(\ker D_5)^J\bmod2=1.
$$

Independently, for the general version let $M$ be a nonempty compact closed oriented Riemannian four-manifold. Let $F^+_{SO}(M)$ be its principal $SO(4)$-bundle of positively oriented orthonormal frames, and specify a spin lift $Q\to F^+_{SO}(M)$, meaning a principal $\operatorname{Spin}(4)$-bundle with an equivariant double covering for $\operatorname{Spin}(4)\to SO(4)$. Use $\operatorname{Spin}(4)=Sp(1)_+\times Sp(1)_-$, where $Sp(1)$ is the unit-quaternion group identified with $SU(2)$ and $(a,b)$ acts on $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$ by $q\mapsto aqb^{-1}$. Let $\Delta^+$ and $\Delta^-$ be the two defining two-dimensional complex half-spin representations, labeled by the Clifford chirality operator $\Gamma=-c(e_1)c(e_2)c(e_3)c(e_4)$ so that it acts by $+1$ on $\Delta^+$ and $-1$ on $\Delta^-$. Define $S^\pm:=Q\times_{\Delta^\pm}\mathbb C^2$. The Clifford action is skew-Hermitian and satisfies $c(v)c(w)+c(w)c(v)=-2g(v,w)$. Let $E\to M$ be a smooth Hermitian rank-two bundle with a specified $SU(2)$ structure and supplied unitary connection $A$, and let $\nabla$ be the tensor-product connection induced by the lifted Levi-Civita connection and $A$. Define the full Dirac operator and its positive chiral restriction by

$$D_A=\sum_{i=1}^4c(e_i)\nabla_{e_i}:H^1(M;S\otimes E)\longrightarrow L^2(M;S\otimes E),\qquad S:=S^+\oplus S^-; \quad D_A^+:=D_A|_{H^1(M;S^+\otimes E)}:H^1(M;S^+\otimes E)\longrightarrow L^2(M;S^-\otimes E),$$

where the displayed local expression is independent of the chosen oriented orthonormal frame. Define $\operatorname{coker}D_A^+:=L^2(M;S^-\otimes E)/\operatorname{ran}D_A^+$. Assume $D_A^+$ is Fredholm; put $n_+=\dim_{\mathbb C}\ker D_A^+$, $n_-=\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}D_A^+$, and $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}D_A^+:=n_+-n_-$. This hypothesis assigns no index value to an arbitrary bundle.

For either fixed four-dimensional background, set $H_+=H^1(M;S^+\otimes E)$ and $H_-=L^2(M;S^-\otimes E)$, and write $\mathfrak F=\operatorname{Fred}(H_+,H_-)$ for the norm-topological space of Fredholm operators from $H_+$ to $H_-$. For a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, define $\det_{\mathbb C}V=\bigwedge^{\dim_{\mathbb C}V}V$ and $\det_{\mathbb C}0=\mathbb C$. Use the inverse determinant-line bundle $\operatorname{Det}^{-1}\to\mathfrak F$ whose fiber at $T\in\mathfrak F$ is

$$\mathcal L_T=(\det_{\mathbb C}\ker T)^*\otimes\det_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{coker}T, \qquad \operatorname{coker}T:=H_-/\operatorname{ran}T.$$

Suppose a connection $\nabla^{\operatorname{Det}}$ on this line bundle is supplied. The central gauge automorphism $z$ fixes $A$ and induces multiplication by $-1$ on both chiral section spaces, hence on $\ker D_A^+$ and $\operatorname{coker}D_A^+$. Its induced fiber map $z_*:\mathcal L_{D_A^+}\to\mathcal L_{D_A^+}$ is the dual top-exterior-power action on $\ker D_A^+$ tensored with the top-exterior-power action on $\operatorname{coker}D_A^+$; thus it acts by $(-1)^{n_++n_-}$. The constant connection path $A_t=A$ gives the constant operator path $\gamma(t)=D_A^+$ in $\mathfrak F$, so parallel transport $\operatorname{PT}_\gamma$ for any supplied line-bundle connection is the identity. For the loop closed by the endpoint gauge identification, the automorphism $z_*^{-1}\circ\operatorname{PT}_\gamma$ is therefore $(-1)^{n_++n_-}=(-1)^{\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}D_A^+}$. On $M\times S^1$ the general product operator is $D_5=D_A+i\Gamma\partial_t$ with periodic domain $H^1$; its real kernel has dimension $n_++n_-$, so its parity is $\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb C}D_A^+\bmod2$. This calculation does not assign an index value to an arbitrary bundle.

In particular, for the explicit round background, the fiber $\mathcal L_{D_A^+}$ has action $-1$, since its chiral kernel dimension is $1$ and cokernel dimension is $0$. The $N$-fold tensor power has action $(-1)^N$. For the fixed product background, antiperiodic total spinor boundary conditions give no product zero mode because a zero mode must be constant in $t$. This distinguishes the tested fermion-parity mapping-torus convention from an automatic eta-holonomy formula. No general spectral-flow or Atiyah–Singer theorem is asserted.

Fix a field $k$. In the ordinary categorical case, a **finite semisimple fusion category over $k$** is a finite semisimple tensor category in the sense of the earlier fusion-and-multifusion definition. Concretely, it is a locally small category (each Hom collection is a set) whose Hom spaces are $k$-vector spaces and whose composition maps are $k$-bilinear. A monomorphism $u:Y\to X$ is a morphism for which precomposition $\operatorname{Hom}(Z,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}(Z,X)$ is injective for every object $Z$; a subobject of $X$ is an isomorphism class of monomorphisms into $X$. An epimorphism is defined by the dual cancellation condition. The category is abelian: it has finite biproducts, kernels, and cokernels, every monomorphism is a kernel, and every epimorphism is a cokernel. Each Hom space is finite-dimensional, and every object has finite length, meaning a finite composition series with simple quotients. A simple object is nonzero with only the zero subobject and itself as subobjects; every object is a finite direct sum of simple objects, and only finitely many simple isomorphism classes occur. It has a $k$-bilinear tensor bifunctor, a tensor unit $\mathbf 1$ with $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf 1)\cong k$, and a natural associator $\alpha_{X,Y,Z}:(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\to X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)$ and left and right unitors satisfying the pentagon and triangle axioms.

For an object $X$, a left dual $X^L$ consists of morphisms $\operatorname{ev}_L:X^L\otimes X\to\mathbf 1$ and $\operatorname{coev}_L:\mathbf 1\to X\otimes X^L$ for which
$$(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes\operatorname{ev}_L)\circ\alpha_{X,X^L,X}\circ(\operatorname{coev}_L\otimes\operatorname{id}_X)=\operatorname{id}_X, \qquad (\operatorname{ev}_L\otimes\operatorname{id}_{X^L})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{X^L,X,X^L}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{X^L}\otimes\operatorname{coev}_L)=\operatorname{id}_{X^L}.$$
A right dual $X^R$ consists of $\operatorname{ev}_R:X\otimes X^R\to\mathbf 1$ and $\operatorname{coev}_R:\mathbf 1\to X^R\otimes X$ for which
$$(\operatorname{ev}_R\otimes\operatorname{id}_X)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{X,X^R,X}\circ(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_R)=\operatorname{id}_X, \qquad (\operatorname{id}_{X^R}\otimes\operatorname{ev}_R)\circ\alpha_{X^R,X,X^R}\circ(\operatorname{coev}_R\otimes\operatorname{id}_{X^R})=\operatorname{id}_{X^R}.$$
The unitors are suppressed in these four composites. Rigidity means that each object has both kinds of dual.

For the ordinary fusion-category clauses below, write $\mathcal C$ for this category.

Choose representatives $i\in I$ of the finitely many simple-object isomorphism classes, with $0\in I$ representing $\mathbf 1$. For each $i,j,\ell\in I$, the **fusion multiplicity** $N_{ij}^{\ell}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ is the number of copies of $\ell$ in a semisimple decomposition of $i\otimes j$, so $i\otimes j\cong\bigoplus_{\ell\in I}N_{ij}^{\ell}\ell$. The associated fusion space is $V_{ij}^{\ell}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(i\otimes j,\ell)$. For $D_\ell:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\ell)$, simplicity makes $D_\ell$ a finite-dimensional division $k$-algebra and $V_{ij}^{\ell}$ a left $D_\ell$-module by postcomposition; its rank as a left $D_\ell$-module is $N_{ij}^{\ell}$. When $D_\ell=k$ (in particular for absolutely simple objects), $\dim_k V_{ij}^{\ell}=N_{ij}^{\ell}$.

For simple $i,j,k,\ell$, the associator induces an isomorphism between the two fusion-channel spaces
$$\bigoplus_{m\in I} V_{mk}^{\ell}\otimes_{D_m}V_{ij}^{m} \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } \bigoplus_{n\in I} V_{in}^{\ell}\otimes_{D_n}V_{jk}^{n}.$$
Here $V_{mk}^{\ell}$ is a right $D_m$-module by $g\cdot d=g\circ(d\otimes\operatorname{id}_k)$, $V_{ij}^{m}$ is a left $D_m$-module by $d\cdot f=d\circ f$, $V_{in}^{\ell}$ is a right $D_n$-module by $f\cdot d=f\circ(\operatorname{id}_i\otimes d)$, and $V_{jk}^{n}$ is a left $D_n$-module by postcomposition. The isomorphism is defined by the semisimple decomposition identifications with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}((i\otimes j)\otimes k,\ell)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(i\otimes(j\otimes k),\ell)$, and the middle map sends $h$ to $h\circ\alpha^{-1}_{i,j,k}$. Thus its domain and codomain are the stated fusion-channel spaces, not unspecified multiplicity symbols. In chosen decompositions and bases these are the associator matrices; their coherence is the pentagon. The fusion datum includes the actual associator, unitors, and both duality structures, not just the integers $N_{ij}^{\ell}$; the unitors satisfy the triangle and the dual maps satisfy the four displayed snake identities.

A **tensor-invertible object** $D$ is an object for which some object $E$ satisfies $D\otimes E\cong\mathbf 1$ and $E\otimes D\cong\mathbf 1$. An object with no such two-sided inverse is **non-invertible**. Simplicity and tensor-invertibility are separate properties: an object can be simple and non-invertible, or a direct sum of invertible simple objects and non-invertible as a whole.

For the **finite semisimple fusion 2-category** convention, assume that $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic zero. A strict $k$-linear 2-category $\mathcal C$ has objects $A,B,\ldots$, a $k$-linear category $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$ for each ordered pair, 1-morphisms as its objects, and 2-morphisms as its morphisms; horizontal composition is $k$-bilinear and strictly associative and unital, and satisfies interchange. A $k$-linear category is one whose morphism spaces are $k$-vector spaces and whose composition is $k$-bilinear. A finite semisimple $k$-linear category is an abelian $k$-linear category with finite-dimensional Hom spaces, finitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects, and every object a finite direct sum of simple objects; in each such category a simple object is nonzero with no nonzero proper subobject, using the ordinary categorical subobject convention above.

A functor between categories is **fully faithful** when it induces a bijection on morphism sets for each pair of objects. For 1-morphisms $p:A\to B$ and $q:B\to A$, an adjunction $p\dashv q$ consists of 2-morphisms (unit) $\eta:\operatorname{id}_A\Rightarrow q\circ p$ and (counit) $\epsilon:p\circ q\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_B$ satisfying $(\epsilon\star p)\cdot(p\star\eta)=\operatorname{id}_p$ and $(q\star\epsilon)\cdot(\eta\star q)=\operatorname{id}_q$, where $\star$ denotes whiskering by 1-morphisms and $\cdot$ denotes vertical composition of 2-morphisms. A 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ is **adjointable** when there are 1-morphisms $l,r:B\to A$ with $l\dashv f\dashv r$, with each adjunction carrying the unit, counit, and triangle identities just specified.

A zero object $0$ is an object for which each Hom category $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,0)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(0,X)$ is equivalent to the zero category, the category with one object and one morphism. A zero 1-morphism is a zero object in its Hom category. A 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ is **fully faithful** when for every object $X$, postcomposition with $f$ gives a fully faithful functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,B)$. A **subobject** of $B$ is an equivalence class of fully faithful 1-morphisms $f:A\to B$, where $f:A\to B$ and $g:A'\to B$ represent the same class exactly when there is an equivalence $u:A\to A'$ and an invertible 2-morphism $g\circ u\Rightarrow f$. A zero subobject is represented by a fully faithful 1-morphism whose domain is equivalent to a zero object. A 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ is an equivalence if there is a 1-morphism $g:B\to A$ and invertible 2-morphisms $g\circ f\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_A$ and $f\circ g\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_B$; two objects are equivalent when there is such an equivalence between them. A nonzero object (one not equivalent to a zero object) is **simple** when all its subobjects are represented by either a zero-domain 1-morphism or an equivalence.

An additive category is a category with a zero object and finite biproducts. A 2-category is **additive** when each Hom category is additive in this sense, it has a zero object, and finite direct sums of objects exist. For $A_1,A_2$, a direct sum $A_1\oplus A_2$ has inclusions $\iota_i:A_i\to A_1\oplus A_2$ and projections $\rho_i:A_1\oplus A_2\to A_i$ with $\rho_i\iota_i\cong\operatorname{id}_{A_i}$, $\rho_i\iota_j$ a zero 1-morphism for $i\ne j$, and $\operatorname{id}_{A_1\oplus A_2}\cong\iota_1\rho_1\oplus\iota_2\rho_2$ in its endomorphism category.

A **monad** on $B$ is a 1-morphism $E:B\to B$ with unit $\eta:\operatorname{id}_B\Rightarrow E$ and multiplication $m:E\circ E\Rightarrow E$ satisfying
$$
m\cdot(\eta\star E)=\operatorname{id}_E=m\cdot(E\star\eta),\qquad m\cdot(m\star E)=m\cdot(E\star m).
$$
It is **separable** when there is an $E$-bimodule 2-morphism $c:E\Rightarrow E\circ E$ such that
$$
c\cdot m=(m\star E)\cdot(E\star c)=(E\star m)\cdot(c\star E),\qquad m\cdot c=\operatorname{id}_E.
$$
The first equation says that $c$ respects the left and right $E$-actions, and the second says that it is a section of multiplication. An isomorphism of monads $\tau:E\Rightarrow F$ is an invertible 2-morphism respecting the units and multiplications: $\tau\cdot\eta_E=\eta_F$ and $\tau\cdot m_E=m_F\cdot(F\star\tau)\cdot(\tau\star E)$.

A **separable splitting** of $E:B\to B$ consists of an object $A$, an adjunction $\rho\dashv\iota$ with $\rho:B\to A$, $\iota:A\to B$, unit $\theta:\operatorname{id}_B\Rightarrow\iota\circ\rho$, and counit $\epsilon:\rho\circ\iota\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_A$, a 2-morphism section $s:\operatorname{id}_A\Rightarrow\rho\circ\iota$ with $\epsilon\cdot s=\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{id}_A}$, and an isomorphism of monads $E\cong\iota\circ\rho$, where $\iota\circ\rho$ has unit $\theta$ and multiplication $\iota\star\epsilon\star\rho$. A 2-category is **finite semisimple** when its Hom categories are finite semisimple, every 1-morphism is adjointable, it is additive, every separable monad has a separable splitting, and it has finitely many equivalence classes of simple objects.

Use the following semistrict monoidal 2-category convention (a Gray monoid). It adds a unit object $I$, strict $k$-linear 2-functors $L_A=A\otimes-$ and $R_A=-\otimes A$ for every object $A$, and for every pair of 1-morphisms $f:A\to A'$ and $g:B\to B'$ an invertible interchanger
$$\phi_{f,g}:(f\otimes B')\circ(A\otimes g)\Rightarrow(A'\otimes g)\circ(f\otimes B).$$
Write $A\otimes B=L_A(B)=R_B(A)$. The tensor is strictly unital and associative: $L_I=R_I=\operatorname{id}$, $L_A L_B=L_{A\otimes B}$, $R_B R_A=R_{A\otimes B}$, and $L_A R_B=R_B L_A$. The interchanger is the identity when either 1-morphism is an identity, is natural in both 2-morphisms, is compatible with composition in each 1-morphism variable, and is compatible with tensoring by an object in either variable. These are coherence axioms on the data, not consequences of a fusion table.

An object $A^R$ is a right dual of $A$ when there are evaluation and coevaluation 1-morphisms $e_R:A\otimes A^R\to I$ and $i_R:I\to A^R\otimes A$ and invertible 2-morphisms exhibiting $(e_R\otimes A)\circ(A\otimes i_R)\cong\operatorname{id}_A$ and $(A^R\otimes e_R)\circ(i_R\otimes A^R)\cong\operatorname{id}_{A^R}$. A left dual $A^L$ has evaluation $e_L:A^L\otimes A\to I$ and coevaluation $i_L:I\to A\otimes A^L$, with invertible 2-morphisms exhibiting $(A\otimes e_L)\circ(i_L\otimes A)\cong\operatorname{id}_A$ and $(e_L\otimes A^L)\circ(A^L\otimes i_L)\cong\operatorname{id}_{A^L}$. A **fusion 2-category** in this convention is a finite semisimple monoidal 2-category in which every object has left and right duals and the monoidal unit is simple.

Neither finite semisimplicity nor either categorical definition asserts unitarity: a dagger structure, positivity, and any unitary coherence are additional hypotheses and data. These are abstract mathematical structures. They do not construct defect operators or junctions in a quantum field theory, specify spacetime support, or prove topological invariance; a physical realization requires a separately specified model and its own construction and proof.

The ordinary associator pentagon below displays the two composites that the axiom requires to agree. This diagram records that axiom; no proof or example verification relies on the drawing.

```tikzcd
& (((W\otimes X)\otimes Y)\otimes Z) \arrow[rr,"\alpha_{W\otimes X,Y,Z}"] \arrow[dl,"\alpha_{W,X,Y}\otimes 1_Z"'] & & (W\otimes X)\otimes(Y\otimes Z) \arrow[dr,"\alpha_{W,X,Y\otimes Z}"] & \\
(W\otimes(X\otimes Y))\otimes Z \arrow[rr,"\alpha_{W,X\otimes Y,Z}"'] & & W\otimes((X\otimes Y)\otimes Z) \arrow[ur,"1_W\otimes\alpha_{X,Y,Z}"'] & & W\otimes(X\otimes(Y\otimes Z))
```

Fix the field data and Minkowski convention from the earlier finite-jet definition, an integer truncation order $N\geq0$, and the truncated coefficient ring $R_N=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{N+1})$. For each regulator label $\rho$, let $X_\rho=X_\rho^{\bar 0}\oplus X_\rho^{\bar 1}$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z/2$-graded complex vector space of field-mode components, with $n_0=\dim_{\mathbb C}X_\rho^{\bar 0}$ and $n_1=\dim_{\mathbb C}X_\rho^{\bar 1}$. Choose even coordinates $q^1,\ldots,q^{n_0}$ and a basis of $X_\rho^{\bar 1}$ whose dual odd coordinate generators are $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n_1}\in(X_\rho^{\bar 1})^*$. Choose a real integration contour $\Gamma_\rho$ in the underlying real space of $X_\rho^{\bar 0}$ and a specified complex-linear functional $\ell_\rho$ on a specified complex algebra $\mathcal C_\rho$ of coefficient functions on $\Gamma_\rho$. The domain $\mathcal C_\rho$ must contain every coefficient function to which $\ell_\rho$ is applied. In an actual integral, $\ell_\rho(f)=\int_{\Gamma_\rho}f\,d\nu_\rho$ for a stated measure $\nu_\rho$ and the coefficients must be integrable; in a formal perturbative integral, $\ell_\rho$ is the stated coefficientwise linear functional and its domain is part of the datum.

The odd-coordinate algebra is the finite exterior algebra $\Lambda(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n_1})$, where $\xi_a\xi_b=-\xi_b\xi_a$ and $\xi_a^2=0$. Put $\mathcal H_\rho=\mathcal C_\rho\otimes\Lambda(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{n_1})$ with graded tensor-product multiplication. For an ordered subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_k\}$, write $\xi_I=\xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_k}$, and set $\xi_\varnothing=1$. Every field-coordinate expression is a finite sum $H=\sum_I f_I\xi_I$. Define the normalized odd-coordinate integration functional by
$$
\mathcal B_\rho(H)=f_{\{1,\ldots,n_1\}},\qquad \mathcal B_\rho(\xi_1\cdots\xi_{n_1})=1.
$$
If $n_1=0$, $\mathcal B_\rho$ is the identity. The full integration functional is $\mathcal I_\rho=\ell_\rho\circ\mathcal B_\rho$, extended coefficientwise to source variables and $R_N$. Thus “integration over odd coordinates” means coefficient extraction in the chosen exterior algebra, not an ordinary integral over odd numbers.

Introduce commuting formal source variables $j_1,\ldots,j_{n_0}$ dual to the even coordinates and independent anticommuting formal source generators $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{n_1}$ dual to the ordered odd coordinates. Their algebra is $\mathscr J_\rho=\mathbb C[\![j_1,\ldots,j_{n_0}]\!]\otimes\Lambda(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_{n_1})$. In these bases the source pairing is
$$
\langle J,\varphi\rangle=\sum_{a=1}^{n_0}j_aq^a+\sum_{b=1}^{n_1}\eta_b\xi_b,
$$
with each odd source placed to the left of its odd field coordinate, so the pairing is even. In particular, $J$ is a graded formal source, not an ordinary element of the complex dual $X_\rho^*$.

A regulated perturbative generating datum also specifies an even action $S_{\rho,\epsilon}\in\mathcal H_\rho\otimes R_N$ and the generating functional
$$
Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]=\mathcal I_\rho\!\left(\exp\!\bigl(iS_{\rho,\epsilon}(\varphi)+i\langle J,\varphi\rangle\bigr)\right),\qquad Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]\text{ is a unit}.
$$
The exponential is interpreted in the chosen convergent or formal algebra: the ordinary exponential is applied to the commuting body and the nilpotent odd and $\epsilon$ parts are expanded finitely. Every coefficient of the generating integrand and of its formal source derivatives must belong to the domain of $\mathcal I_\rho$. “A unit” means that the $\epsilon^0$ coefficient of $Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]$ is nonzero; hence the normalized functional $\widehat Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]=Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]/Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[0]$ is defined in $\mathscr J_\rho\otimes R_N$ and has constant term $1$ at $J=0$.

For an ordered list of source components, define the connected $n$-point kernel as $i^{-n}$ times the corresponding ordered source derivatives of $\log\widehat Z_{\rho,\epsilon}[J]$ at $J=0$. Even-source derivatives are ordinary derivatives. Odd-source derivatives are left graded derivatives, characterized by $\partial^L_{\eta_a}\eta_b=\delta_{ab}$ and
$$
\partial^L_{\eta_a}(UV)=(\partial^L_{\eta_a}U)V+(-1)^{|U|}U(\partial^L_{\eta_a}V)
$$
for homogeneous $U,V$. The logarithm is the formal logarithm with zero constant term. The regulator datum supplies the reconstruction of the component kernels as spacetime kernels and a Fourier-transform convention. The Fourier transform is $\widetilde f(p)=\int e^{ip\cdot x}f(x)\,d^4x$, interpreted in the specified function or distribution space.

An admissible field-coordinate change is a local, parity-preserving formal map $F_{\rho,\epsilon}$ on these graded coordinates with $F_{\rho,0}=\operatorname{id}$ and an inverse modulo $\epsilon^{N+1}$. If the coordinates come from spacetime fields, local means that each output field at $x$ depends on a finite jet of the input fields at $x$. Its regulated Jacobian factor $\mathcal J_{F,\rho}$ is a multiplier in the field-coordinate algebra specified by the exact graded change-of-variables identity
$$
\mathcal I_\rho(h(\varphi))=\mathcal I_\rho\!\left(h(F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi))\,\mathcal J_{F,\rho}(\psi)\right)
$$
for every admissible integrand $h$, with the functional extended coefficientwise over $\mathscr J_\rho\otimes R_N$. No assertion that $\mathcal J_{F,\rho}=1$ is part of the definition. For the standard product of an even-coordinate measure and the stated Berezin functional, this factor is the Berezinian: if the graded derivative has block form $DF=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$ with $D$ invertible, then $\operatorname{Ber}(DF)=\det(A-BD^{-1}C)(\det D)^{-1}$. In the transformed coordinates the source is $\langle J,F_{\rho,\epsilon}(\psi)\rangle$, so the field insertion remains the same named original coordinate.

An LSZ amplitude datum is an additional common regulator limit of the connected momentum-space Green functions, when that limit exists. For each external one-particle channel $a$ (with a fixed polarization component when the field has spin), the datum specifies a mass $m_a>0$ and nonzero simple-pole residue $Z_a$ at $s_a=m_a^2$, where $s_a=-\eta^{\mu\nu}p_{a,\mu}p_{a,\nu}$. A stable external channel means precisely that this isolated pole exists with nonzero residue and zero width. For each selected field-parity sector, the datum supplies finite lists of interpolating-field components $A$ and one-particle channels $a$, together with scalar entries $U_{Aa}\in\mathbb C$ called their field-to-channel overlap coefficients; the square matrix $U$ must be invertible. For every ordered $n$-point component function it requires pole factorization
$$
G_n(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{Z_{a_j}^{1/2}}{s_j-m_{a_j}^2}\right)\mathcal A_n(p_1,\ldots,p_n)+\text{terms missing at least one external pole}.
$$
The normalized LSZ amplitude is the joint residue
$$
\mathcal A_n=\left(\prod_{j=1}^n Z_{a_j}^{-1/2}\right)\lim_{s_j\to m_{a_j}^2}\left(\prod_{j=1}^n(s_j-m_{a_j}^2)\right)G_n,
$$
with the overall momentum-conservation delta function removed and the same ordered graded-source convention as above. The joint limits, Fourier transforms, pole factorization and invertible overlap data must all exist as part of the supplied LSZ datum. This definition supplies only the regulator and pole data needed for a conditional amplitude statement. It does not assert that a continuum limit, stable particles, or LSZ poles exist for a given quantum field theory.

Fix a field $k$. In the ordinary categorical case, a **finite semisimple fusion category over $k$** is a finite semisimple tensor category in the sense of the earlier fusion-and-multifusion definition. Concretely, it is a locally small category (each Hom collection is a set) whose Hom spaces are $k$-vector spaces and whose composition maps are $k$-bilinear. A monomorphism $u:Y\to X$ is a morphism for which precomposition $\operatorname{Hom}(Z,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}(Z,X)$ is injective for every object $Z$; a subobject of $X$ is an isomorphism class of monomorphisms into $X$. An epimorphism is defined by the dual cancellation condition. The category is abelian: it has finite biproducts, kernels, and cokernels, every monomorphism is a kernel, and every epimorphism is a cokernel. Each Hom space is finite-dimensional, and every object has finite length, meaning a finite composition series with simple quotients. A simple object is nonzero with only the zero subobject and itself as subobjects; every object is a finite direct sum of simple objects, and only finitely many simple isomorphism classes occur. It has a $k$-bilinear tensor bifunctor, a tensor unit $\mathbf 1$ with $\operatorname{End}(\mathbf 1)\cong k$, and a natural associator $\alpha_{X,Y,Z}:(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\to X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)$ and left and right unitors satisfying the pentagon and triangle axioms.

For an object $X$, a left dual $X^L$ consists of morphisms $\operatorname{ev}_L:X^L\otimes X\to\mathbf 1$ and $\operatorname{coev}_L:\mathbf 1\to X\otimes X^L$ for which
$$(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes\operatorname{ev}_L)\circ\alpha_{X,X^L,X}\circ(\operatorname{coev}_L\otimes\operatorname{id}_X)=\operatorname{id}_X, \qquad (\operatorname{ev}_L\otimes\operatorname{id}_{X^L})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{X^L,X,X^L}\circ(\operatorname{id}_{X^L}\otimes\operatorname{coev}_L)=\operatorname{id}_{X^L}.$$
A right dual $X^R$ consists of $\operatorname{ev}_R:X\otimes X^R\to\mathbf 1$ and $\operatorname{coev}_R:\mathbf 1\to X^R\otimes X$ for which
$$(\operatorname{ev}_R\otimes\operatorname{id}_X)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{X,X^R,X}\circ(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_R)=\operatorname{id}_X, \qquad (\operatorname{id}_{X^R}\otimes\operatorname{ev}_R)\circ\alpha_{X^R,X,X^R}\circ(\operatorname{coev}_R\otimes\operatorname{id}_{X^R})=\operatorname{id}_{X^R}.$$
The unitors are suppressed in these four composites. Rigidity means that each object has both kinds of dual.

For the ordinary fusion-category clauses below, write $\mathcal C$ for this category.

Choose representatives $i\in I$ of the finitely many simple-object isomorphism classes, with $0\in I$ representing $\mathbf 1$. For each $i,j,\ell\in I$, the **fusion multiplicity** $N_{ij}^{\ell}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ is the number of copies of $\ell$ in a semisimple decomposition of $i\otimes j$, so $i\otimes j\cong\bigoplus_{\ell\in I}N_{ij}^{\ell}\ell$. The associated fusion space is $V_{ij}^{\ell}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(i\otimes j,\ell)$. For $D_\ell:=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\ell)$, simplicity makes $D_\ell$ a finite-dimensional division $k$-algebra and $V_{ij}^{\ell}$ a left $D_\ell$-module by postcomposition; its rank as a left $D_\ell$-module is $N_{ij}^{\ell}$. When $D_\ell=k$ (in particular for absolutely simple objects), $\dim_k V_{ij}^{\ell}=N_{ij}^{\ell}$.

For simple $i,j,k,\ell$, the associator induces an isomorphism between the two fusion-channel spaces
$$\bigoplus_{m\in I} V_{mk}^{\ell}\otimes_{D_m}V_{ij}^{m} \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } \bigoplus_{n\in I} V_{in}^{\ell}\otimes_{D_n}V_{jk}^{n}.$$
Here $V_{mk}^{\ell}$ is a right $D_m$-module by $g\cdot d=g\circ(d\otimes\operatorname{id}_k)$, $V_{ij}^{m}$ is a left $D_m$-module by $d\cdot f=d\circ f$, $V_{in}^{\ell}$ is a right $D_n$-module by $f\cdot d=f\circ(\operatorname{id}_i\otimes d)$, and $V_{jk}^{n}$ is a left $D_n$-module by postcomposition. The isomorphism is defined by the semisimple decomposition identifications with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}((i\otimes j)\otimes k,\ell)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(i\otimes(j\otimes k),\ell)$, and the middle map sends $h$ to $h\circ\alpha^{-1}_{i,j,k}$. Thus its domain and codomain are the stated fusion-channel spaces, not unspecified multiplicity symbols. In chosen decompositions and bases these are the associator matrices; their coherence is the pentagon. The fusion datum includes the actual associator, unitors, and both duality structures, not just the integers $N_{ij}^{\ell}$; the unitors satisfy the triangle and the dual maps satisfy the four displayed snake identities.

A **tensor-invertible object** $D$ is an object for which some object $E$ satisfies $D\otimes E\cong\mathbf 1$ and $E\otimes D\cong\mathbf 1$. An object with no such two-sided inverse is **non-invertible**. Simplicity and tensor-invertibility are separate properties: an object can be simple and non-invertible, or a direct sum of invertible simple objects and non-invertible as a whole.

For the **finite semisimple fusion 2-category** convention, assume that $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic zero. A strict $k$-linear 2-category $\mathcal C$ has objects $A,B,\ldots$, a $k$-linear category $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$ for each ordered pair, 1-morphisms as its objects, and 2-morphisms as its morphisms; horizontal composition is $k$-bilinear and strictly associative and unital, and satisfies interchange. A $k$-linear category is one whose morphism spaces are $k$-vector spaces and whose composition is $k$-bilinear. A finite semisimple $k$-linear category is an abelian $k$-linear category with finite-dimensional Hom spaces, finitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects, and every object a finite direct sum of simple objects; in each such category a simple object is nonzero with no nonzero proper subobject, using the ordinary categorical subobject convention above.

A functor between categories is **fully faithful** when it induces a bijection on morphism sets for each pair of objects. For 1-morphisms $p:A\to B$ and $q:B\to A$, an adjunction $p\dashv q$ consists of 2-morphisms (unit) $\eta:\operatorname{id}_A\Rightarrow q\circ p$ and (counit) $\epsilon:p\circ q\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_B$ satisfying $(\epsilon\star p)\cdot(p\star\eta)=\operatorname{id}_p$ and $(q\star\epsilon)\cdot(\eta\star q)=\operatorname{id}_q$, where $\star$ denotes whiskering by 1-morphisms and $\cdot$ denotes vertical composition of 2-morphisms. A 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ is **adjointable** when there are 1-morphisms $l,r:B\to A$ with $l\dashv f\dashv r$, with each adjunction carrying the unit, counit, and triangle identities just specified.

A zero object $0$ is an object for which each Hom category $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,0)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(0,X)$ is equivalent to the zero category, the category with one object and one morphism. A zero 1-morphism is a zero object in its Hom category. A 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ is **fully faithful** when for every object $X$, postcomposition with $f$ gives a fully faithful functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,B)$. A **subobject** of $B$ is an equivalence class of fully faithful 1-morphisms $f:A\to B$, where $f:A\to B$ and $g:A'\to B$ represent the same class exactly when there is an equivalence $u:A\to A'$ and an invertible 2-morphism $g\circ u\Rightarrow f$. A zero subobject is represented by a fully faithful 1-morphism whose domain is equivalent to a zero object. A 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ is an equivalence if there is a 1-morphism $g:B\to A$ and invertible 2-morphisms $g\circ f\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_A$ and $f\circ g\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_B$; two objects are equivalent when there is such an equivalence between them. A nonzero object (one not equivalent to a zero object) is **simple** when all its subobjects are represented by either a zero-domain 1-morphism or an equivalence.

An additive category is a category with a zero object and finite biproducts. A 2-category is **additive** when each Hom category is additive in this sense, it has a zero object, and finite direct sums of objects exist. For $A_1,A_2$, a direct sum $A_1\oplus A_2$ has inclusions $\iota_i:A_i\to A_1\oplus A_2$ and projections $\rho_i:A_1\oplus A_2\to A_i$ with $\rho_i\iota_i\cong\operatorname{id}_{A_i}$, $\rho_i\iota_j$ a zero 1-morphism for $i\ne j$, and $\operatorname{id}_{A_1\oplus A_2}\cong\iota_1\rho_1\oplus\iota_2\rho_2$ in its endomorphism category.

A **monad** on $B$ is a 1-morphism $E:B\to B$ with unit $\eta:\operatorname{id}_B\Rightarrow E$ and multiplication $m:E\circ E\Rightarrow E$ satisfying
$$
m\cdot(\eta\star E)=\operatorname{id}_E=m\cdot(E\star\eta),\qquad m\cdot(m\star E)=m\cdot(E\star m).
$$
It is **separable** when there is an $E$-bimodule 2-morphism $c:E\Rightarrow E\circ E$ such that
$$
c\cdot m=(m\star E)\cdot(E\star c)=(E\star m)\cdot(c\star E),\qquad m\cdot c=\operatorname{id}_E.
$$
The first equation says that $c$ respects the left and right $E$-actions, and the second says that it is a section of multiplication. An isomorphism of monads $\tau:E\Rightarrow F$ is an invertible 2-morphism respecting the units and multiplications: $\tau\cdot\eta_E=\eta_F$ and $\tau\cdot m_E=m_F\cdot(F\star\tau)\cdot(\tau\star E)$.

A **separable splitting** of $E:B\to B$ consists of an object $A$, an adjunction $\rho\dashv\iota$ with $\rho:B\to A$, $\iota:A\to B$, unit $\theta:\operatorname{id}_B\Rightarrow\iota\circ\rho$, and counit $\epsilon:\rho\circ\iota\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_A$, a 2-morphism section $s:\operatorname{id}_A\Rightarrow\rho\circ\iota$ with $\epsilon\cdot s=\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{id}_A}$, and an isomorphism of monads $E\cong\iota\circ\rho$, where $\iota\circ\rho$ has unit $\theta$ and multiplication $\iota\star\epsilon\star\rho$. A 2-category is **finite semisimple** when its Hom categories are finite semisimple, every 1-morphism is adjointable, it is additive, every separable monad has a separable splitting, and it has finitely many equivalence classes of simple objects.

Use the following semistrict monoidal 2-category convention (a Gray monoid). It adds a unit object $I$, strict $k$-linear 2-functors $L_A=A\otimes-$ and $R_A=-\otimes A$ for every object $A$, and for every pair of 1-morphisms $f:A\to A'$ and $g:B\to B'$ an invertible interchanger
$$\phi_{f,g}:(f\otimes B')\circ(A\otimes g)\Rightarrow(A'\otimes g)\circ(f\otimes B).$$
Write $A\otimes B=L_A(B)=R_B(A)$. The tensor is strictly unital and associative: $L_I=R_I=\operatorname{id}$, $L_A L_B=L_{A\otimes B}$, $R_B R_A=R_{A\otimes B}$, and $L_A R_B=R_B L_A$. The interchanger is the identity when either 1-morphism is an identity, is natural in both 2-morphisms, is compatible with composition in each 1-morphism variable, and is compatible with tensoring by an object in either variable. These are coherence axioms on the data, not consequences of a fusion table.

An object $A^R$ is a right dual of $A$ when there are evaluation and coevaluation 1-morphisms $e_R:A\otimes A^R\to I$ and $i_R:I\to A^R\otimes A$ and invertible 2-morphisms exhibiting $(e_R\otimes A)\circ(A\otimes i_R)\cong\operatorname{id}_A$ and $(A^R\otimes e_R)\circ(i_R\otimes A^R)\cong\operatorname{id}_{A^R}$. A left dual $A^L$ has evaluation $e_L:A^L\otimes A\to I$ and coevaluation $i_L:I\to A\otimes A^L$, with invertible 2-morphisms exhibiting $(A\otimes e_L)\circ(i_L\otimes A)\cong\operatorname{id}_A$ and $(e_L\otimes A^L)\circ(A^L\otimes i_L)\cong\operatorname{id}_{A^L}$. A **fusion 2-category** in this convention is a finite semisimple monoidal 2-category in which every object has left and right duals and the monoidal unit is simple.
